nodes.label: Web framework
nodes.description: Framework for building and deploying web applications, services, resources and APIs.

nodes.label: Web application framework
nodes.description: Alternative name for a web framework.

nodes.label: Web development framework
nodes.description: Alternative name for a web framework.

nodes.label: Web application
nodes.description: Application delivered through web technologies.

nodes.label: Web service
nodes.description: Network-accessible service a framework may help create.

nodes.label: Web resource
nodes.description: Addressable resource exposed by a web application or service.

nodes.label: Web API
nodes.description: Programmatic interface exposed through web protocols.

nodes.label: World Wide Web
nodes.description: Environment in which frameworks standardize web application development.

nodes.label: Code reuse
nodes.description: Reuse of common implementation patterns and libraries.

nodes.label: Database access
nodes.description: Facilities for reading and writing persistent data.

nodes.label: Web templating
nodes.description: Mechanisms for constructing web output from templates.

nodes.label: Session management
nodes.description: Maintains application interaction state across stateless HTTP requests.

nodes.label: Dynamic website
nodes.description: Site whose responses depend on inputs or application logic.

nodes.label: Static website
nodes.description: Site serving static content; frameworks can also support static sites.

nodes.label: HTML
nodes.description: Markup used by early hand-authored pages and browser output.

nodes.label: Web server
nodes.description: Server publishing pages and interfacing with applications.

nodes.label: Common Gateway Interface (CGI)
nodes.description: 1993 standard connecting external applications with web servers for dynamic pages.

nodes.label: Per-request process creation
nodes.description: Original CGI implementations often created a separate process for each request, increasing server load.

nodes.label: Persistent processes
nodes.description: Later approaches reused processes and other techniques to reduce resource footprint.

nodes.label: Full-stack framework
nodes.description: Cohesive stack combining multiple web-development libraries; mature examples appeared in the late 1990s per source.

nodes.label: Software library
nodes.description: Reusable code component that a framework can include or orchestrate.

nodes.label: Model–view–controller (MVC)
nodes.description: Pattern separating model/domain concerns, view presentation and controller coordination.

nodes.label: Model
nodes.description: Data/domain behavior and business concerns in the broad source description.

nodes.label: View
nodes.description: Presentation layer rendering information for a user or client.

nodes.label: Controller
nodes.description: Coordinates request/action processing and interaction with model/view concerns.

nodes.label: Business logic
nodes.description: Rules and domain behavior of the application.

nodes.label: User interface
nodes.description: User-facing representation of application information.

nodes.label: Push-based / action-based architecture
nodes.description: Actions process a request and push data to the view.

nodes.label: Pull-based / component-based architecture
nodes.description: View starts the flow and pulls results from one or more controllers.

nodes.label: Action
nodes.description: Processing unit used in push-based architectures.

nodes.label: Three-tier organization
nodes.description: Client, application and database tiers. Distinct from MVC.

nodes.label: Client tier
nodes.description: Browser or other client consuming application output.

nodes.label: Application tier
nodes.description: Server tier containing business logic and communicating with client using HTTP.

nodes.label: Database tier
nodes.description: Persistence tier, normally an RDBMS in the source description.

nodes.label: Relational database management system
nodes.description: Typical database technology in the described three-tier organization.

nodes.label: HTTP
nodes.description: Stateless protocol used between browser/client and application server.

nodes.label: Web browser
nodes.description: Runs HTML and can update pages using JavaScript.

nodes.label: JavaScript
nodes.description: Language used for browser-side page changes and client-side frameworks.

nodes.label: Server-side page changes
nodes.description: Server-generated changes typically require a page refresh; can use server resources and many languages.

nodes.label: Client-side page changes
nodes.description: Browser JavaScript updates parts of the page without a full reload; constrained by client resources.

nodes.label: Single-page application (SPA)
nodes.description: JavaScript-heavy app that refreshes only parts of the page and typically uses a client-side framework.

nodes.label: Mixed server/client rendering
nodes.description: Combination of server-side and client-side techniques, described as typical.

nodes.label: Server-side web frameworks
nodes.description: Examples grouped in the source server-side list.

nodes.label: Client-side web frameworks
nodes.description: Examples grouped in the source client-side list.

nodes.label: Inversion of control
nodes.description: Framework sets program flow and exposes hooks/events for application code.

nodes.label: Framework-controlled flow
nodes.description: Framework owns the general lifecycle and invokes extension points.

nodes.label: Hooks and extension points
nodes.description: Events or callbacks where application code plugs into framework flow.

nodes.label: Middleware
nodes.description: Logic run before or after HTTP requests, such as logging, authentication, sessions or redirects.

nodes.label: Logging
nodes.description: Recording request or application activity.

nodes.label: Authentication
nodes.description: Verifying or identifying a user.

nodes.label: Authorization
nodes.description: Restricting access to functions or resources.

nodes.label: Role-based access control
nodes.description: Permissions assigned through roles; Drupal is given as an example.

nodes.label: Web cache
nodes.description: Stores copies of web documents for subsequent requests when conditions allow.

nodes.label: Cache hit
nodes.description: Request can be satisfied from stored cached output.

nodes.label: Cache miss
nodes.description: Cached output cannot satisfy request, so further processing is required.

nodes.label: Bandwidth usage
nodes.description: Caching aims to reduce data transfer.

nodes.label: Server load
nodes.description: Caching and persistent processes can reduce resource demand.

nodes.label: Perceived latency
nodes.description: Caching aims to reduce perceived lag.

nodes.label: Template interpretation
nodes.description: Page-preparation stage that caching may bypass.

nodes.label: Object–relational mapping (ORM)
nodes.description: Maps application objects to relational tuples/records.

nodes.label: Database backend
nodes.description: Specific database implementation hidden behind a common API.

nodes.label: Unified database API
nodes.description: Common database interface can reduce backend-specific application code.

nodes.label: Application object
nodes.description: Object-oriented representation mapped by ORM.

nodes.label: Relational tuple
nodes.description: Relational record representation.

nodes.label: Hibernate
nodes.description: Java persistence layer cited as capable of runtime schema generation.

nodes.label: Introspection
nodes.description: Inspecting application structures to reduce explicit configuration.

nodes.label: Convention over configuration
nodes.description: Use conventions to minimize manual setup.

nodes.label: Database schema
nodes.description: Structure of persistent data.

nodes.label: Active Record
nodes.description: Rails persistence layer cited for mapping objects to tables and providing data methods.

nodes.label: Database transactions
nodes.description: Frameworks may provide transactional support.

nodes.label: Database migrations
nodes.description: Tools for evolving database schemas over time.

nodes.label: URL mapping / routing
nodes.description: Interprets URLs and maps them to application behavior.

nodes.label: URL pattern matching
nodes.description: Matches incoming URLs against predetermined patterns, sometimes regular expressions.

nodes.label: Regular expression
nodes.description: Pattern technique cited for Django and Drupal routing.

nodes.label: URL rewriting
nodes.description: Transforms a supplied URL into a form recognized by an application engine.

nodes.label: Graph-traversal routing
nodes.description: Decomposes URL into steps through an object graph of models and views; Zope is cited.

nodes.label: Zope
nodes.description: Framework cited for graph-traversal URL mapping.

nodes.label: Friendly URL
nodes.description: Shorter, human-readable URL produced through routing or rewriting.

nodes.label: Search-engine indexing
nodes.description: Friendly URLs can make site structure clearer to search engines.

nodes.label: Ajax (Asynchronous JavaScript and XML)
nodes.description: Exchanges small amounts of data in the background to update parts of a page without a full reload.

nodes.label: Partial page update
nodes.description: Updates a page region without reloading the entire document.

nodes.label: Ajax framework
nodes.description: Framework dedicated to Ajax support or embedded in a larger framework.

nodes.label: jQuery
nodes.description: Article says jQuery is included in Rails as an Ajax-support example.

nodes.label: Morfik
nodes.description: Compiler technology cited for high-level-language rich Ajax applications.

nodes.label: Google Web Toolkit
nodes.description: Toolkit cited for compiling high-level-language applications for the web.

nodes.label: Pyjs
nodes.description: Python-oriented port named in the Ajax compiler history.

nodes.label: RubyJS
nodes.description: Ruby-oriented port named in the Ajax compiler history.

nodes.label: Web-service tools
nodes.description: Utilities for creating and providing web services.

nodes.label: Resource-oriented architecture (ROA)
nodes.description: Approach for exposing collections of resources through web services.

nodes.label: Resource Description Framework (RDF)
nodes.description: Concepts cited in the article resource-oriented architecture discussion.

nodes.label: Semantic Web ontology
nodes.description: Ontology-like organization of resources described in the article.

nodes.label: Native web standards
nodes.description: Browser standards and APIs that can reduce the need for framework-specific abstractions.

nodes.label: Web Components
nodes.description: Native web standard emphasized by Enhance.dev in the article.

nodes.label: Fetch API
nodes.description: Modern JavaScript API listed as a native web capability.

nodes.label: ECMAScript modules
nodes.description: Native module system listed as a modern web capability.

nodes.label: Shadow DOM
nodes.description: Browser capability listed among native standards.

nodes.label: Framework abstraction layers
nodes.description: Can improve structure but may add overhead, bundle size and complexity.

nodes.label: Bundle size
nodes.description: Framework abstraction can increase shipped client code size.

nodes.label: Performance overhead
nodes.description: Runtime/resource costs that can accompany framework abstractions.

nodes.label: Developer productivity
nodes.description: Structured patterns and tooling are cited benefits.

nodes.label: Performance optimization
nodes.description: Frameworks may provide tools to improve application performance.

nodes.label: Concurrent rendering
nodes.description: Named as an approach used in modern React/Vue to address rendering challenges.

nodes.label: Tree-shaking
nodes.description: Optimization that removes unused code.

nodes.label: Selective hydration
nodes.description: Selective client activation of server-rendered output.

nodes.label: Virtual DOM
nodes.description: Svelte is described as eliminating this abstraction in favor of compilation.

nodes.label: Svelte
nodes.description: Compiles components to efficient JavaScript and is described as eliminating the virtual DOM.

nodes.label: Preact
nodes.description: Minimal compatible alternative to React in the source description.

nodes.label: React
nodes.description: Client-side JavaScript framework example; also discussed in modern trade-offs.

nodes.label: Vue.js
nodes.description: Client-side framework; Vue 3 features are mentioned in the trade-off discussion.

nodes.label: Fresh
nodes.description: Focuses on server-side rendering; source describes zero runtime overhead.

nodes.description: Emphasizes progressive enhancement and Web Components.

nodes.label: Progressive enhancement
nodes.description: Builds on native web standards while adding interactivity where needed.

nodes.label: Server-side rendering
nodes.description: Generates page output on the server.

nodes.label: Hydration
nodes.description: Client-side activation of interactive server-rendered output.

nodes.label: Static HTML

nodes.label: Zero runtime overhead

source_claims.claim: A web framework supports development of web applications, services, resources and APIs.
Frameworks may provide database access, templating and session management and promote code reuse.
Article history moves from hand-coded HTML to CGI, integrated language environments and full-stack frameworks.
Many frameworks are described as using MVC and supporting modularity and multiple views.
Push actions send data to views; pull views retrieve results from controllers.
Three-tier organization separates client, application and database and is not equivalent to MVC.
Server-side, client-side and mixed rendering have distinct trade-offs.
Article lists server-side and client-side framework examples.
Framework abstractions can add overhead, bundle size and complexity.
Astro, Fresh and Enhance.dev are described as approaches using SSR, selective hydration or progressive enhancement.
Frameworks control program flow and expose hooks; middleware can run around HTTP requests.
Caching may reduce bandwidth, server load and perceived lag.
Some frameworks provide authentication/authorization; Drupal illustrates role-based access.
Frameworks may provide unified DB APIs, ORM, introspection, transactions and migrations.
Routing can use patterns, rewriting or graph traversal.
Ajax exchanges background data to update parts of a page without full reload.
Some frameworks provide web-service tools and resource-oriented infrastructure.
Article says it needs more citations and unsourced claims may be challenged.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Framework controls the broad flow and exposes hooks; a library is reusable code called by application code.
MVC separates software responsibilities; three-tier separates client, application and database tiers.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Avoids mixing code architecture and deployment tiers.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Push sends action results to views; pull starts at the view and retrieves controller results.
Server changes commonly refresh pages; client JavaScript can update fragments but depends on browser resources.
Frameworks often target dynamic sites but can also support static sites.
Framework is a development structure; SPA is an application architecture that often uses a client-side framework.
A hit can serve cached output when conditions permit; a miss continues processing.
Authentication verifies identity; authorization controls access.
ORM maps objects to records; unified API abstracts backend differences.
Pattern matching compares URLs; rewriting transforms URLs; graph traversal follows an object graph.
Ajax background exchange updates page regions without reloading the entire document.
Native standards advanced, while frameworks still offer productivity and structure at possible runtime/bundle cost.
Svelte is described as compiling components to JavaScript and eliminating the virtual DOM.
SSR generates output; hydration activates client interactivity, potentially only in selected regions.
Article statements are source-reported; synthesized flows are labelled as models.
Framework owns the lifecycle; middleware is custom logic inserted at defined points.
Frameworks can improve developer productivity while adding bundle size, abstraction cost or complexity.
Some frameworks provide auth capabilities; this does not prove secure defaults or eliminate vulnerabilities.

misconceptions.misconception: A framework is just a library.
misconceptions.correction: The article emphasizes framework-controlled flow and hooks as inversion of control.

misconceptions.misconception: MVC and three-tier architecture are the same.
misconceptions.correction: MVC separates software responsibilities; three-tier separates client, application and database.

misconceptions.misconception: Frameworks only work for dynamic sites.
misconceptions.correction: The article says frameworks can also apply to static sites.

misconceptions.misconception: All frameworks render only on the server.
misconceptions.correction: The article distinguishes server-side and client-side approaches and says mixed approaches are common.
An SPA is an application architecture that often uses a client-side framework.
The article describes HTTP as stateless and session management as a separate framework capability.

misconceptions.misconception: A cache always serves the request.
misconceptions.correction: Cached copies satisfy requests only when cache conditions are met.
Authentication verifies identity; authorization controls access.

misconceptions.misconception: ORM and unified DB API are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: ORM maps objects to records; unified API abstracts database backends.
The article describes pattern matching, rewriting and graph traversal.

misconceptions.misconception: Ajax requires a full page reload.
misconceptions.correction: Ajax exchanges data in the background and updates page regions.
Abstractions can add overhead, bundle size and complexity; outcomes depend on context.

misconceptions.misconception: Modern standards make all frameworks unnecessary.
misconceptions.correction: The article says frameworks remain useful for productivity, structure and edge cases.

misconceptions.misconception: Every frontend framework uses a virtual DOM.
misconceptions.correction: Svelte is described as compiling components and eliminating the virtual DOM.

misconceptions.misconception: Fresh zero-runtime-overhead is an independently verified benchmark.
misconceptions.correction: It is a source characterization, not a measurement verified here.
